findings.quote: The **context** is the occasion, place, and time of the speech.
findings.problem: ustet-L064 (official curriculum) names speech context and speech style. The DepEd Oral Communication competencies are to identify the types of speech context (intrapersonal, interpersonal, public, mass) and to distinguish the types of speech style (intimate, casual, consultative, formal, frozen). The lesson defines context only as occasion, place and time and teaches a two-way formal or casual split, so neither set of curriculum types is taught or worked. The brief's limit already names context-type distinctions as untaught.
findings.source: Brief, ustet-L064 and item 'Interpret speech context/style distinctions'; DepEd SHS Oral Communication in Context curriculum guide (2016), 'Types of Speech Context and Style', EN11/12OC-Ifj-15

findings.quote: If the purposes are mixed, pick the one the ending of the excerpt serves.
findings.problem: The shortcut has no limit. An excerpt can be cut anywhere, and a speech can end with a closing courtesy or request that is not its main purpose (a commemorative speech that ends 'Please join us for refreshments'). It also differs from Core Concept, which asks what the speaker most wants by the end of the speech, not of the excerpt.
findings.source: Checklist L27; writer rules after round 1, rule 4 (word every shortcut with its limit)

findings.quote: Check its source, method, and relevance before you credit it as logos.
findings.problem: The lesson mixes up which appeal a passage uses with how strong that appeal is. Example #5 likewise says 'If the evidence is accurate and fairly interpreted, the main appeal is **logos**', but Example #6 labels an unchecked statistic logos with no condition. A weak or irrelevant statistic is still an appeal to logos, only a weak one. Because the lesson never says so, a student asked to name the appeal of a dubious statistic may wrongly reject logos.
findings.source: Checklist L27; internal contradiction between Example #5, Example #6 and Trap #1

findings.quote: A **speech** is spoken language addressed to an audience. A **scripted** speech is written out in advance and read or recited.
findings.problem: This Core Concept paragraph has four sentences, above the one-to-three limit. Other four-sentence paragraphs: the paragraph starting 'In this lesson you read printed excerpts', the paragraph starting 'Common purposes are to inform', the paragraph starting 'These appeals can overlap', and the paragraph starting 'A **repair strategy**'.

findings.quote: The phrase "We will rebuild" recurs, which is **repetition**. The three sentences also share one pattern, so they form **parallelism** too.
findings.problem: The solution makes two separate identifications, repetition and then parallelism, in one paragraph instead of a numbered list. No step is skipped, so this is Minor.
